title: R CMD check failures: local_mock() defunct, snapshot mismatches, ggplot2 compat
description:
R CMD check is failing on macOS (ARM64, R release), Windows (R release), and Windows (R 3.6) with 9 test failures. Failures are pre-existing and unrelated to recent doc changes. ## Failure summary ``` [ FAIL 9 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 2006 ] ``` ## Three root causes ### 1. `local_mock()` defunct (testthat ≥ 3.2.0) `test-graded.R` calls `testthat::local_mock()`, which is now defunct and errors immediately. ``` Error: `local_mock()` was deprecated in testthat 3.2.0 and is now defunct. i Please use `local_mocked_bindings()` instead. ``` **Fix:** Replace `local_mock(...)` with `local_mocked_bindings(...)` in `test-graded.R`. ### 2. Snapshot mismatches Several snapshots in `test-graded.R` are stale — error message formatting changed (likely a testthat or rlang update). Run `testthat::snapshot_review()` to accept or update. ### 3. testthat error message format changes `test-code_feedback.R` expects error messages matching `"\\.result.+has type.+I expected"` but the actual format has changed to HTML-style output (`

Expected .result...`). ### 4. ggplot2 compat `test-call_standardise_formals.R` has a failure related to ggplot2 function call standardisation, likely the same ggplot2 S7 migration affecting ggcheck (#40). ## Spotted via CI on the `exit-netlify` PR (#367) but pre-existing on `main`.

title: Can `gradethis::grade_this` use checks on the provided code (not the evaluated results)
description:
I know I can test for an exact match on a student's code using `grade_this_code()` but is there a way to check for an exact match on what was typed as an answer on the code using `grade_this()`.   

I am working on teaching students about the type of vectors used by R.  I want students to use `typeof()` to realize that R returns the _major version_ of R as a character string (because it is a number that will not be used for math):
````
```{r ex2-typeof-solution, exercise.reveal_solution = TRUE}
typeof(R.version$major)
```
````
I see students providing: `typeof(R.version$nickname)` as a solution.  That, like the correct answer of `typeof(R.version$major)`, returns a character string.  So it is being called a correct answer.  

Is there a way to trap the case that students type a specific response inside of `grade_this()`?  I think you can see what I am getting at using this code

````
```{r ex2-typeof-check}
grade_this({
  # I want to see if they typed this text
  fail_if_equal(.user_code == "typeof(R.version$nickname)", 
    message = "You are checking the nickname you want to be checking the major"
  )
  pass_if_equal(typeof(R.version$major), 
    message = "Interesting the version number is being treated as a character string. R does not want you to do math on the version number."
  )
  fail_if_equal(R.version$major,
    message = "Your code is telling you the major version. You want to check the type using `typeof()`."              
  )
  fail_if_equal(R.version,
    message = "That code tells you everything about the R version. Add a `$` and the key word for the `major` version."              
  )  
  fail(message = "Not quite. Take a peek at the hints!")
})
```
````


I see that `.user_code` captures the provided text but I don't see how to use it in a logic check.

title: `call_standardise_formals()` fails when calling `map()` with an index rather than a function
description:
``` r
list <- list(
  c(1, 2),
  c("a", "b")
)

call <- quote(purrr::map(list, 2))

gradethis:::call_standardise_formals(call)
#> Error in `rlang::call2()`:
#> ! Can't create call to non-callable object
#> Backtrace:
#>     ▆
#>  1. ├─gradethis:::call_standardise_formals(call)
#>  2. │ └─gradethis:::call_standardise_passed_arguments(...)
#>  3. │   └─gradethis:::dot_args_standardise(...)
#>  4. │     └─rlang::call2(f_arg, x_arg, !!!dot_args)
#>  5. └─rlang::abort(message = message)
```

<sup>Created on 2023-06-13 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

This occurs because the internal function `call_standardise_passed_arguments()` attempts to turn the call `map(.x, .f, ...)` into a call to `.f(.x[[1]], ...)` in order to determine the default arguments in `...`. When `.f` is not a function, this call cannot be created.

title: `pass_if_equal()` does not pass when `.result` and `.solution` are the same `ggplot`
description:
`pass_if_equal()` detects a difference between two identical `ggplot`s if one has been printed and one has not.
Because `.result` is shown to the student and `.solution` is not, this will almost always be the case.

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(gradethis)

plot_code <- quote(
  ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class)) + 
    geom_point()
)

.result   <- eval(plot_code)
.solution <- eval(plot_code)

# Passes if both plots have not been print
pass_if_equal()
#> <gradethis_graded: [Correct] That's a first-class answer! Correct!>

.result
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/IhgCZ1e.png)

``` r

# Fails if one plot has been printed
pass_if_equal()
#> NULL

.solution
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/np11qpU.png)<!-- -->

``` r

# Passes if both plots have been printed
pass_if_equal()
#> <gradethis_graded: [Correct] Superb work! Correct!>
```

<sup>Created on 2023-05-04 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

This is because printing a `ggplot` adds additional computed data to each layer:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(gradethis)

plot_code <- quote(
  ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class)) + 
    geom_point()
)

.result   <- eval(plot_code)
.solution <- eval(plot_code)

.result
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/6dbX1kb.png)<!-- -->

``` r

waldo::compare(.result, .solution)
#> `old$layers[[1]]` is length 15
#> `new$layers[[1]]` is length 12
#> 
#>     names(old$layers[[1]]) | names(new$layers[[1]])    
#> [1] "aes_params"           | "aes_params"           [1]
#> [2] "computed_geom_params" -                           
#> [3] "computed_mapping"     -                           
#> [4] "computed_stat_params" -                           
#> [5] "constructor"          | "constructor"          [2]
#> [6] "data"                 | "data"                 [3]

#> 
#> `old$layers[[1]]$computed_geom_params` is a list
#> `new$layers[[1]]$computed_geom_params` is absent
#> 
#> `old$layers[[1]]$computed_mapping` is an S3 object of class <uneval>, a list
#> `new$layers[[1]]$computed_mapping` is absent
#> 
#> `old$layers[[1]]$computed_stat_params` is a list
```

title: `grade_this_code()` duplicates feedback when `gradethis_setup(fail.hint = TRUE)`
description:
When `gradethis_setup(fail.hint = TRUE)`, `grade_this_code()` provides the same feedback twice when given an incorrect answer. This is most likely because `grade_this_code()` internally calls two functions that can generate feedback: `code_feedback()` and `fail()`.

``` r
library(gradethis)
ex <- mock_this_exercise(.user_code = "sqrt(log(2))", .solution_code = "sqrt(log(1))")

gradethis_setup(fail.hint = FALSE)
grade_this_code()(ex)
#> <gradethis_graded_this_code: [Incorrect]
#>   In `log(2)`, I expected `1` where you wrote `2`. That's okay: you
#>   learn more from mistakes than successes. Let's do it one more time.
#> >

gradethis_setup(fail.hint = TRUE)
grade_this_code()(ex)
#> <gradethis_graded_this_code: [Incorrect]
#>   In `log(2)`, I expected `1` where you wrote `2`. Try it again. You
#>   get better each time. In `log(2)`, I expected `1` where you wrote
#>   `2`.
#> >
```
<sup>Created on 2022-09-30 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

## Possible solution
`grade_this_code()` could internally call `fail(hint = FALSE)` to ensure that `fail()` never generates a duplicate message.

title: `fail(hint = TRUE)` gives multiple hints in exercises with multiple solutions
description:
`fail(hint = TRUE)` generates a hint for all solutions in exercises with multiple solutions.It should only generate one hint for the solution closest to the user input.

``` r
library(gradethis)

solution_code <- "
# mean ----
mean(1:10)
# median ----
median(1:10)"
```

`fail(hint = TRUE)` generates two hints: one for each solution.

```r
grade_this({
  pass_if_equal()
  fail(hint = TRUE)
})(
  mock_this_exercise("sum(1:10)", !!solution_code)
)
#> <gradethis_graded: [Incorrect]
#>   Incorrect. I expected you to call `mean()` where you called `sum()`.
#>   Try it again. You get better each time. I expected you to call
#>   `median()` where you called `sum()`.
#> >
```

`fail_if_code_feedback()` behaves as expected: it only generates one hint.

```r
grade_this({
  pass_if_equal()
  fail_if_code_feedback()
})(
  mock_this_exercise("sum(1:10)", !!solution_code)
)
#> <gradethis_graded: [Incorrect]
#>   I expected you to call `mean()` where you called `sum()`.
#> >
```

title: Duplicated encouragement when global `fail.encourage = TRUE` is enabled
description:
Basic setup where `fail.encourage = TRUE` is turned on globally.

``` r
library(gradethis)

gradethis_setup(
  fail.encourage = TRUE,
  fail = "\n\nDEFAULT FAIL MESSAGE. {random_encouragement()}"
)
```

I’m going to mask learnr’s random encouragement messages to make it easier to see the duplication.

``` r
options(tutorial.language = "test")
withr::with_options(
  list(knitr.in.progress = FALSE),
  learnr::random_phrases_add("test", encouragement = "RANDOM ENCOURAGEMENT")
)
```

A basic exercise (do you know the answer to life, etc.).

``` r
ex <- mock_this_exercise(.user_code = 43, .solution_code = 42)
```

Calling `fail_if()` with `encourage = TRUE` (the default) results in duplicated encouragement.

``` r
grade_this({
  fail_if(
    identical(.result, 43),
    "FEEDBACK FOR SPECIFIC CASE.",
    encourage = TRUE
  )
})(ex)
#> <gradethis_graded: [Incorrect]
#>   FEEDBACK FOR SPECIFIC CASE. RANDOM ENCOURAGEMENT RANDOM ENCOURAGEMENT
#> >
```

Calling `fail_if()` with `encourage = FALSE` suppresses the duplicated encouragement.

``` r
grade_this({
  fail_if(
    identical(.result, 43),
    "FEEDBACK FOR SPECIFIC CASE.",
    encourage = FALSE
  )
})(ex)
#> <gradethis_graded: [Incorrect]
#>   FEEDBACK FOR SPECIFIC CASE. RANDOM ENCOURAGEMENT
#> >
```

In `fail_if()` we call [`maybe_extras()`](https://github.com/rstudio/gradethis/blob/4fbbd004d407c6c528d41e16f0dbef3646bb8a92/R/graded.R#L842) https://github.com/rstudio/gradethis/blob/4fbbd004d407c6c528d41e16f0dbef3646bb8a92/R/graded.R#L556-L561 which should suppress one of the random encouragement messages.

title: Add gradethis_default() lookup helper
description:
Currently, we lookup gradethis options via `getOption("gradethis.fail", "Fall back default")`, which has a few disadvantages:

- the correct fallback needs to be used in every case
- it clutters the API since the preferred method for setting the defaults is via `gradethis_setup()`
- it isn't easy to differentiate between actively supplied arguments and default values determined from global settings without resorting to sentinel values that further obscure the mechanics

We should add a helper for looking up global default values: `gradethis_default()`

```r
fail <- function(
  message = gradethis_default("fail"),
  ...,
  hint = gradethis_default("fail.hint"),
  encourage = gradethis_default("fail.encourage")
) { ... }
```

where the documentation can better direct users to `gradethis_setup()` where those values are set since both functions would be documented in the same help page.

Internally, `gradethis_default()` could add an `attr()` that we could use to determine whether or not the argument value was supplied by the user or looked up from global options.

title: Should we remove maybe_code_feedback()?
description:
Currently we can use `maybe_code_feedback()` in the default `fail()` message, which can be turned on or off via the `fail_code_feedback()` argument of `grade_this()` or the `gradethis.fail_code_feedback` option.

I don't like that this argument only has an effect on the output **if and only if** `maybe_code_feedback()` was used for the default message.

The motivation for it to exist is that it's otherwise difficult to adjust the default values of the `fail()` message. This makes sense, but maybe we should take a different approach:

1. Use the `...` and `with_options()` to let users temporarily set options for the current exercise check
2. Get rid of `maybe_code_feedback()` and `fail_code_feedback` and have the user adjust the default fail message.

This leads to (maybe) a bit more typing but gives the user more control. It's been hard to explain the many ways that `fail()`, `code_feedback()`, `maybe_code_feedback()`, `gradethis.fail` and `gradethis.fail_code_feedback` and to ensure they appear in the documentation in a discoverable and understandable way.

title: Update gradethis_setup() signature (breaking change)
description:
I'm still a bit unsatisfied with the current state of `gradethis_setup()`. Especially now that it isn't strictly required, it bugs me that the first arguments are all setting learnr options instead of gradethis options.

Instead of

```r
gradethis_setup <- function(
  exercise.timelimit = NULL,
  exercise.checker = NULL,
  exercise.error.check.code = NULL,
  ...,
  pass = NULL,
  fail = NULL,
  code_correct = NULL,
  code_incorrect = NULL,
  fail_code_feedback = NULL,
  pipe_warning = NULL,
  allow_partial_matching = NULL
) {
 #...
}
```

I'd like to propose


```r
gradethis_setup <- function(
  pass = NULL,
  fail = NULL,
  ...,
  code_correct = NULL,
  code_incorrect = NULL,
  fail_code_feedback = NULL,
  pipe_warning = NULL,
  allow_partial_matching = NULL,
  exercise.checker = gradethis_exercise_checker,
  exercise.timelimit = NULL,
  exercise.error.check.code = NULL
) {
 #...
}
```

With this new signature, `pass` and `fail` come first as they're the most likely to be customized. `...` are still passed to `learnr::tutorial_options()` but also serve to require full argument names. gradethis options come next, followed by learnr options. I've also added the default values of the `exercise.checker` option, since this value will always be set by `gradethis_setup()` unless given another value.

It's hard to judge the impact of this change, but I haven't found any publicly available examples of `gradethis_setup()` using custom values, so I doubt the impact will be large.

title: Align .onLoad and gradethis_setup()
description:
AFAICT `.onLoad()` does the same work as `gradethis_setup()`, but because some arguments of `gradethis_setup()` differ from the default options in `gradethis_default_options`, these two processes might be at odds with each other.

```r
library(gradethis)
getOption("gradethis.code.incorrect")
#> [1] "{pipe_warning()}{code_feedback()} {random_encouragement()}"
```

``` r
gradethis::gradethis_setup()
#> Loading required package: gradethis
getOption("gradethis.code.incorrect")
#> [1] "{ .message } { random_encouragement() }"
```

I think we should have `gradethis_setup()` operate more like `learnr::tutorial_options()`. So running

```r
library(gradethis)
gradethis_setup()
```

would be equivalent to

```r
library(gradethis)
```

Effectively, `gradethis_setup()` arguments would all default to `NULL`. The function would set non-`NULL` arguments or fill in unset arguments with the default values. Then `gradethis_default_options` becomes the source of truth about the default option values, but we would document all of the options and their meaning in `gradethis_setup()`.

@schloerke the one piece that's confusing me at the moment is why it's necessary for gradethis to set knitr options in `.onload()` rather than settings the `learnr::tutorial_options()` as in `gradethis_setup()`?

title: Environment for evaluation of .solution
description:
Because `.solution` is delay-assigned, it's possible to pass it on to other functions where it's ultimately evaluated in the wrong environment.

Here's a simple reprex. Submitting the answer returns `object 'x' not found` because `.solution` refers to `x` from the setup chunk.

````markdown
```{r example-setup}
x <- 1
```

```{r example, exercise=TRUE}
# user submits
x + 3
```

```{r example-solution}
x + 3
```

```{r example-check}
grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(.solution)
  fail()
})
```
````

Changing the grading code to the following fixes the issue, but I suspect this won't be obvious and will cause issues down the line, and really this treats the symptom not the problem.

````
```{r example-check}
grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(force(.solution))
  fail()
})
```
````

Here's the kicker, though. I'm fairly certain that the real issue is that `envir_prep` doesn't actually contain the results of the exercise setup chunk, just the global setup chunk.

````
```{r example-check}
grade_this({
  message(str(list(envir_prep = pryr::rls(.envir_prep))))
  pass_if_equal(.solution)
  fail()
})
```
````

Running that through the solution check gives

````
 $ envir_prep:List of 2
  ..$ : chr [1:3] ".server_context" ".shiny_prerendered_server_start_code" "same"
  ..$ : chr [1:4] ".First" ".Random.seed" "dput_to_string" "same"
````

where no `x` is defined. `.envir_prep` should be the same environment where `solution_expr` is evaluated.

https://github.com/rstudio-education/gradethis/blob/a07ecfee1e64578efba35f3aa62744d08806db82/R/grade_learnr.R#L130-L133

To the end user, this result in a message in the tutorial

title: Document magic variables
description:
I want to document and standardize the environment and glue variables that are exposed to users.

## Environment Variables

These variables can be accessed in `grade_this()` checking blocks and used by `pass()`/`fail()` and `{pass,fail}_if_equal()` messages.

### Check Environment

The check environment includes several special variables that are used both for checking the exercise and can be accessed by the template strings:

- `.label`: the label of the current exercise
- `.engine`: the code engine for the current exercise (typically `"r"`)
- `.user_code`: a string with the user's submitted code
- `.last_value`: the last value returned when executing the user's submitted code
- `.user`: a copy of `.last_value`
- `.result`: a copy of `.last_value`
- `.solution_code`: a string with the solution code
- `.solution`: the value returned when executing the solution code (delayed evaluation to avoid computation if not needed)
- `.error`: When the user code fails to parse, `.error` will contain the parse error object
    - Only available to the parse error function defined in the global option `exercise.parse.error`
- `.envir_prep`: the environment prior to running the submitted code, i.e. global `setup` + exercise `-setup` chunks
- `.envir_result`: the environment _after_ running the submitted code

## Message Variables

These are places where templates strings (intended for `glue()`) are defined and the special variables that may be available to them.

### Pipe Message

- Global Option: `gradethis_glue_pipe`
- Used in
   - `grade_code()`, `glue_pipe` argument
   - `grade_this_code()`, `glue_pipe` argument
- Magic variables
   - `.user_code` the user submission as a character string
   - `.user_code_unpiped` the user submission, rewritten without pipes
- Notes
   - After #193 
   - The glue pipe message becomes `.message_pipe_warning`

description:
I'd like to be able to safely create objects in `grade_result()` to use in my `pass_if()` and `fail_if()` checks. Here is an example, the fictitious `setup` argument takes a chunk of code that will be run in the same environment that the `fail_if()` checks will be run in. The `setup` code is run before these checks, so the checks can rely on its output, greatly magnifying the number of things I can check. I assume that the parent of this environment is the student's environment after the student code has run. I also assume that `.result` is available to code run in this environment. 

```r
grade_result(
   setup = {
     .solution <- iris %>% filter(Species == "Setosa")
     .common_error <- iris %>% filter(Species == "Virginica")
     .max <- .result %>% pluck("Sepal.Length) %>% max()
   },
   fail_if(~nrow(.result) != nrow(.solution), "custom message 1"),
   fail_if(~ncol(.result) != ncol(.solution), "custom message 2"),
   fail_if(~names(.result) != names(.solution), "custom message 3"),
   fail_if(~identical(.result, .common_error), "You filtered the wrong group"),
   fail_if(~.max == 1.3, "custom message 4"),
)
```

title: Add "send to grade_code" option to fail_if
description:
`grade_code()` attempts to provide a useful suggestion to the student about how to fix their code. Often, authors will want to provide this message in addition to the message that accompanies a `fail_if()` condition. i.e. 

* The `fail_if()` message explains why the result is wrong
* The `grade_code()` method suggests a way to get back on track

Alternatively, for some `fail_if()` checks an author may want to suppress a `grade_code()` message. This will be particularly true for cases where there are multiple ways to solve the exercises and it will be relatively obvious what wen wrong.

To facilitate thid, we should provide a way for authors to indicate that failing code should be compared to the solution to generate an additional feedback message with `grade_code()`

title: Default feedback for "fill in the blanks" blanks left in exercise
description:
Many tutorial authors use exercises where they have a "fill in the blanks" type scaffolding for learners to start with, e.g.

```r
ggplot(data = ___, aes(x = mpg, y = ___) +
  ___
```

Usually, these are 3 underscores, but different authors might use different placeholders for the blanks.

It would be nice if gradethis had a default message if learner left any `___` in their submission, like _"Please replace all blanks with valid code."_ It's a bit of a pain to write code checking for existence of blanks and makes the `-check` chunk repetitive throughout the document, and this would help. I think tutorial authors would be fine if the package required a certain type of representation for blanks (e.g., 3 underscores) but it might also be nice if the authors could set a gradethis option within a tutorial to indicate the text string they're using to indicate blanks.

title: grade_code throws error when user code contains unused argument
description:
For example, the code below returns an error, which prevents `grade_code()` from telling the student what he or she did wrong:

````r
a <- function(x) x
grade_code(
  grader_args = list(
    user_quo = quote(a(1, y = b(1))),
    solution_quo = quote(a(1, y = a(1)))
  )
)
## Error in match.call(definition, call, expand.dots, envir) : 
## unused argument (y = b(1)) 
````

The error is the result of `rlang::call_standardise()` calling `match.call()` which throws the error when there are unused arguments.

title: grade_conditions should return a message when a condition fails
description:
As it is written, `grade_conditions()` does not provide formative feedback (feedback that can help the student diagnose what he or she did wrong). 

To fix this, `grade_conditions()` should return the message argument of _every_ unpassed check. To avoid the confusion of having `pass_if()` messages address correct answers in `grade_result()` and incorrect answers in `grade_conditions()`, we should either: 

1. Replace `pass_if()` with `fail_if()` in `grade_conditions()`

or 

2. Preface the messages with, "Your result did not satisfy the following conditions:"

The upside of the second is that it models unit testing, the downside is that explaining what went unmet in human friendly terms does not necessarily tell the student how to fix it. However, if the messages need to teach, the teacher should use `grade_results()` with a series of `fail_ifs()`.

title: check_code should not require use of `standardise_call`
description:
It's confusing and hard to test.  There should never be a "it's voodoo" when explaining how it works.

Current:
```r
check_result(args, grader_args, learnr_args) # checks result
```

Proposed:
```r
ck_fn <- check_result(args) # returns function that accepts grader_args / learnr_args
ck_fn # will be called after "*-check" evaluation as `ck_fn(grader_args, learnr_args)`
```


This allows for any function to be produced in any way as long as a function is returned from the chunk that accepts `grader_args` and `learnr_args`.  We do not need to be cautious of parameter expansion as `grader_args` is already included and is a list.

This would require functions like `check_result` to return a function that does the evaluation.  Rough example:

```r
new_check_result(...) {
  results <- list(...)

  function(grader_args, learnr_args) {
    # check results here

    graded(TRUE)
  }
}
```


This would clean up the logic inside grade_learnr and would be much easier to enforce / document

title: launch tutorial at startup
check_result API
description:
Grader is going through some API changes in #10 .  Thank you all for your input and patience!

Two big motivations are at play: keep it simple (@garrettgman ), keep it clean (@wch ).

---------------------------------------------

After talking it through with @blairj09, I think we have a clean, simple solution for `check_result`.
* Two check object functions: `passes` and `fails`.  (These names do not class with `checkmate` or `testthat`.)
* `passes` and `fails` can take:
  * a Value - equivalent to `~ identical(., value)`
  * a Formula - Evaluate the formula with `.` representing the user result
    * By using a formula (purrrr style) with `.`, there is no non-standard evaluation trickery to understand (such as a random `ans` being available).  As long as we state that `.` is the user result, the validation can be processed however the user writes.
    * Should return `TRUE` / `FALSE`
    * Throwing will cause an error in computing (bad for author)
  * a Function that takes an user result argument
    * Should return `TRUE` / `FALSE`
    * Throwing will cause an error in computing (bad for author)
* Once an equality (against a value) is found or `TRUE` (from a formula / function) is returned, computation will stop.  The respective message will be displayed as a correct (`passes`) or incorrect (`fails`) result.
* `correct` or `incorrect` params will be the default message for any `passes` or `fails` that do not provide a message.  They will be `glue`ed with appropriate information.

Example:

```r
check_result(
  fails(5, "bad answer!"),
  fails(~ . == 5, "bad answer!"),
  fails(~ isTRUE(all.equal(., 5)), "bad answer!"),
  fails(~ . %in% c(5,7), "bad answer!"),
  fails(function(x) x == 5, "bad answer!"),
  fails(function(x) x == 5),
  fails(somepkg::some_method, "bad answer!"), # function(x) ...

  passes(4, "good answer!"),
  passes(~ . == 4, "good answer!"),
  passes(~ . %in% c(4,6), "good answer!"),
  passes(function(x) x == 4, "good answer!"),
  passes(function(x) x == 4),
  passes(somepkg::some_method, "good answer!"), # function(x) ...

  correct = "You got it right!",
  incorrect = "You got it wrong."
)
```

---------------------------------------------

`check_result` will be kept separate from `test_result`.  All tests will be executed for `test_result`. 
* `test_result` will take
  *  a `test` object which will only accept formulas or functions as defined above (no values).  The message supplied will be provided if any throw occurs.
  * a Formula - the thrown error will be reported
  * a Function - the thrown error will be reported
* `correct` and `incorrect` will be `glue`ed with appropriate information.

Example:
```r
test_result(

  ~ checkmate::assert_function(., args = "x"),
  test(~ checkmate::assert_function(., args = "x"), "Make sure to have an 'x' argument!"),
  somepkg::some_expectation, # function(x) ...
  pryr::partial(checkmate::assert_function, args = "x"),

  correct = "{num_correct} / {num_total} correct! {random_praise()}",
  incorrect = "{num_correct} / {num_total} correct. {random_encourage()}"
)
```

---------------------------------------------

Again, these are not set in stone... just a followup from discussions over the past 48 hrs.

cc @gvwilson
